title: Program 1: The Entangled Mind
seed_question: Does encoding a language model's competing claims as an entangled quantum state flag its wrong answers better than classical controls?
note: Structure and open paths only. Where a node lists bets, its verdict, odds and dates come from ledger/bets.jsonl, never from this file. Phase A nodes (before the ledger began) carry their outcome here, taken from entangled-mind paper/record.md. Sources: paper/record.md, paper/gold-map.md (eae3975), paper/biomimetic-map.md (144f07e, f824e14). Open nodes carry cockpit fields (question, known, cheapest_test, odds_event) for site/cockpit.html. moved_to marks a direction carried into another program's map, which the cockpit shows there instead.

directions.title: H1: does the encoding faithfully hold the model's claims?
H2, the primary: does the entangled readout flag the model's wrong answers?
directions.diagnosis: The entangled readout did worse than every classical control (AUROC 0.55 against 0.64–0.68), and noise is not the cause.

directions.title: H3 and H4: do the entanglement and the relation web carry information?
directions.diagnosis: Both falsified. The real relation web scored below 99% of 200 shuffled webs.

directions.title: H5: do the entangled states survive real quantum hardware?
directions.result: Entanglement certified on 3 of 3 items on ibm_fez (46 QPU s).

directions.title: Does the model's own stated confidence carry the error signal?
directions.result: Stated confidence (0.82) beat every structural arm.

directions.title: Does a learned quantum encoding beat a matched classical twin?
directions.diagnosis: A tie, 0.83 against 0.84. The fit set the couplings near zero: it switched entanglement off itself.

directions.title: Does an honest-hedge encoding help?
directions.diagnosis: Not met, 0.84 against 0.82. The hedge weight fitted to zero; the hedge was not the problem.

directions.title: Is the edge on Sonnet's errors entanglement?
directions.diagnosis: No. The edge is a per-claim readout angle; a classical twin matches it exactly and setting couplings to zero changes nothing.

directions.title: Experiment 3: do quantum or classical predictions track yes/no order effects?
directions.diagnosis: Inconclusive. The model is near-deterministic: 85% of items give the same answer in all five runs.

directions.title: Experiment 4: do the model's ratings follow the Yearsley–Trueblood quantum rules?
directions.result: Conjunction fallacies on 7 of 16 items and order effects of about +0.10, but the mechanism is undetermined.

directions.title: Anchoring or content-driven updating, with a provided first rating?
directions.diagnosis: Untestable. The model resists a first rating it is given: in 15 of 32 item-orders it never accepted one.

directions.title: Experiment 5: does a quantum belief state predict sequential ratings better than a matched classical updater?
directions.diagnosis: A tie. A dephased classical Markov chain matches the quantum state; no QQ or Kvam signature.

directions.title: Are the graded order effects real, on one scale direction?
directions.result: Yes: a median 25-point swing, surviving one scale direction (12 of 16 large pairs). The live finding grew from here.

directions.question: When two questions sit close together inside the model, does asking them in a different order move its answers more?
known: Order really does move the model's ratings: a median 25-point swing on one scale.
Our own encoder's geometry failed to predict where order effects appear (1 win, 2 losses); the model's own was never measured.
directions.cheapest_test: On an open model, measure how close about 100 claim pairs sit internally, and check whether that predicts each pair's order effect better than a simple anchoring rule.
directions.odds_event: Internal overlap predicts the size of the order effect beyond the classical anchoring predictor.

directions.title: Gold map 10: post-quantum belief geometry on natural text, or contextuality at scale
directions.question: Are the model's beliefs stored in a shape that ordinary probability cannot describe?
known: Our graded ratings show almost no contextuality: 1 pair in 80; another study also found none.
Networks trained on toy processes show quantum-like belief shapes; natural text is untested.
directions.cheapest_test: Look at the internal belief geometry of an open model on natural text and test whether it falls outside the ordinary probability shape.
directions.odds_event: Natural-text belief states lie outside the classical probability simplex.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.0/3.1: does a number pull harder when framed as the model's own earlier answer?
Source × distance × lag: does own-over-other hold at other distances and after a delay?
Biomimetic 3.1: confidence-gated confirmation toward another person's number
Biomimetic 3.10: does the next rating move toward or away from the last number?
Biomimetic 3.4: is the model sampling probabilities (PT+N identity)?
Biomimetic 3.5: do serial-position weights rule out competing accumulators (LCA)?
Biomimetic 3.3: precision weighting (predictive coding)
directions.question: Does a hint about base rates move the model's shaky beliefs more than its confident ones?
known: Stated confidence carries the error signal as well as any structural model (0.82 to 0.91).
The brain theory behind this (precision weighting) is a simulation, with no data of its own.
directions.cheapest_test: Rate the 160 claims under two base-rate hints, ten repeats each, and check whether the shift is bigger where stated confidence is low.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.6: bounded accumulation and 2DSD
directions.question: Does the model's confidence keep improving after it has already given its answer?
known: Making a choice midway did not change later confidence (no human-sized effect).
People's confidence keeps building after a choice; the published prediction here is not unique.
directions.cheapest_test: Ask the model to reconsider, or give it a filler task, after its answer, and check whether its confidence tracks the truth better.

directions.title: Biomimetic 3.7: second-order metacognition (Fleming & Daw)
directions.question: After the model commits to an answer, does its confidence get better at telling right from wrong?
known: The other half of this theory already failed: choosing did not lower later confidence.
The 450 conversations with and without a choice are archived, so this costs nothing.
directions.cheapest_test: Using the archived conversations, compare how well the final rating separates true from false answers with a choice made versus without.
directions.odds_event: The final rating's AUROC is higher with a midway choice (K1) than without (K0).

directions.title: Sean's biomimicry queue, a scout item: memory, sleep and adaptive forgetting against catastrophic forgetting (open-weight only)
directions.question: Can the way brains forget on purpose, in sleep, stop a model forgetting what it learned before?
known: Not yet scouted. Only an open model can be tested, since training is needed.
The field is crowded: memory replay and complementary learning systems are well studied.
directions.cheapest_test: A scout session (operators/scout.md): full reads across neuroscience and continual learning, next steps extracted, each candidate costed; no test is designed until the scout returns.
directions.odds_event: A full-read scout of the queue (complementary learning systems, sleep-like replay, adaptive forgetting, catastrophic forgetting in continual learning) returns at least one direction with a cheapest falsifier under $5 that runs on an open-weight model on the laptop and that the scout's reads show has not already been run.
directions.cost: $0 API; one scout session of reading
directions.source: CONTEXT.md section 5 (Sean's biomimicry queue); steer st-14
directions.odds_template: none: stated in one pass by the close-founding session (branch close-founding), not by the scout's v1 fresh-context template; re-elicit with v1 before pre-registration
directions.odds_rationale: The field is crowded (replay-based continual learning, complementary learning systems, mortal computation), so most cheap tests will already exist; and anything involving training needs an open model and compute we only have locally. Kept above 0.25 because program 1's own finding (consistency is carried by the transcript) gives an angle the continual-learning literature does not take.

engine_only: the scout returns three or more such directions: engine odds 0.10

directions.short: Entangled claims: quantum walk vs PageRank
directions.title: Sean's entangled-claims idea: does a quantum walk over program 1's claim graph predict which of its directions were killed and which hit, better than PageRank does?
directions.odds_template: none: stated in one pass by the close-founding session (branch close-founding), not by the scout's v1 fresh-context template; re-elicit with v1 before pre-registration
directions.odds_event: On program 1's claim graph (the directions in map/entangled-mind.json as nodes, parent links and shared-data/replication links as edges), a continuous-time quantum walk started from the known hits and kills, scored leave-one-node-out, predicts each resolved node's outcome (hit 1, killed 0; mixed and open left out) with AUROC higher than personalised PageRank on the same graph and the same seeds, by a bootstrap 95% interval whose lower end is above 0. Quantum counts only if it beats this classical baseline; beating chance alone does not count.
directions.odds_rationale: Program 1 put six quantum-against-classical comparisons on the record (h2, h34, v2, v21, son, e5) and the classical twin matched or won every one: (0+1)/(6+2) = 0.125 by the running-base-rate rule (P1). Lower again because about 25 labelled nodes on a near-tree give little power, and on a tree a quantum walk's ranking and a diffusion's are close. Odds are for beating PageRank, not for beating chance.
directions.question: Can the way program 1's ideas connect to each other, treated as a quantum system, tell which of them were going to fail, better than ordinary link-ranking can?
known: Program 1's quantum-against-classical tests: the classical twin matched or won all six.
The claim graph and every outcome are already in the ledger, so the test costs nothing; the quantum walk is simulated on the laptop, no chip.
directions.cheapest_test: Archive only: build the graph from map/entangled-mind.json and ledger/bets.jsonl, run a simulated continuous-time quantum walk and personalised PageRank from the same seeds, hide one resolved node at a time, and compare the two AUROCs at predicting kill or hit. Pre-register the walk time, the PageRank damping and the edge list before the outcomes are joined.
directions.cost: $0 API; laptop minutes; no chip time (the walk is a simulation, invariant 9)
directions.human_prompt: Is it worth a few minutes of laptop time (free) to treat program 1's ideas as a connected quantum system, and see whether that tells which ideas were going to fail better than ordinary link-ranking (the way search engines rank pages) does? Will it come back a hit (here, a hit means the quantum version beats ordinary link-ranking, not just chance)?
engine_only: PageRank alone predicts kills and hits above chance (AUROC interval above 0.5): engine odds 0.15
the quantum walk alone predicts above chance: engine odds 0.12 (correlated with the PageRank sub-bet)
